newsitem.title: VIETNAM: After trial, narcotics menace remains in Vietnam.
newsitem.headline: After trial, narcotics menace remains in Vietnam.

text.p: A day after a sensational narcotics trial ended in Hanoi with death sentences for eight people, drugs experts warned on Thursday that more needed to be done to tackle a growing heroin scourge in Vietnam.
The eight sentenced to death on Wednesday included police and border officials.
Another 14 people were given jail sentences as the trial ended with scenes of near chaos outside the court building where police held hundreds of onlookers at bay.

But less than 24 hours after the verdicts, the media frenzy that had been growing for weeks had died away. Near hysterical coverage afforded to the trial was reduced to mostly straightforward details of sentencing.
Analysts warned that without further action, the propaganda benefits of a case which gripped the nation's attention for days might be similarly short-lived.
"This trial alone will not make it (trafficking rings) stop because outside elements are involved," said Ngo Ba Thanh, vice president of the Vietnam Lawyers Association.
"Vietnamese law alone cannot stop this. The problem has reached an international level and what we need now is regional and international cooperation."
Drugs usage and trafficking have grown sharply in Vietnam in recent years in tandem with the country's efforts to open its borders and overcome near isolation during the late 1970s and early 1980s.
But the problem, plus the involvement of mafias and local government or security officials, are age-old problems, both in Vietnam and in the region as a whole.

Opium has been produced and consumed in Indochina for centuries. In areas such as the Golden Triangle -- where the borders of Burma, China, Laos and Thailand meet -- it continues to be used by groups or individuals as a political tool.

But drugs experts in Hanoi said that situation did not apply to Vietnam, where evidence suggested the problem was more purely a criminal one despite the involvement of members of the national security establishment in this week's trial.
"This case was significant in that it took place and because people (officials) at that level were brought to court," said Joern Kristensen of the United Nations Drugs Control Programme (UNDCP).
"(But) The next step is to establish cooperation between Vietnam and China. Laos too has a prominent role to play, although that may be more difficult."
Vietnam is a member of the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN). Three other countries, Burma, Laos and Cambodia are expected to become members soon, possibly this year.

Analysts said that participation of these countries in a regional grouping would help combat trafficking through increased sharing of intelligence, but they said nationalism and mistrust might remain obstacles.
"The history of wars in this region which have divided neigbours means that historical suspicions need to be overcome," Kristensen said.
"In the short term this trial will have helped, but in the long term it has to be followed up internationally, and inside Vietnam with a more active policy on preventative education."
